title: Muslims in America
hookLine: immigrants, converts and African American Muslims, a very diverse community

cards: Friday, just after noon, in a mosque in an American city. A man in a Detroit auto plant jacket. A doctor whose parents came from Lahore.
A grandmother whose family has been Black and Muslim in Philadelphia for generations. A young woman from a Lutheran family in Minnesota who became Muslim in college. A Somali taxi driver.
A Bosnian baker. They stand in one row, and nobody needs to ask where anyone is really from. The answer, for all of them, is here.

teach.b: American Muslims are a very varied community, and three big streams run into it.

The first is immigrants. Arab families settled in the Midwest and worked in factories; South Asians came as doctors, engineers and students; later came people from Iran, Turkey, Bosnia, Somalia and many other places.
The second is African American Muslims. Two days ago we met enslaved Africans who prayed in chains. Slavery made that faith hard to hand down.

Later, Black Americans found their way to Islam again, through several movements. Some passed through the Nation of Islam, and under Warith Deen Mohammed much of that community turned to mainstream Sunni practice.
The third stream is converts of every background, who walked into a mosque one day and said the shahada. Here's the idea worth keeping.

For the people in that Friday row, American and Muslim are not two halves pulling apart. They are one life. The boxer Muhammad Ali took the name, prayed, fought, joked, and was American to his fingertips.

teach.h: THERE IS NO COMPULSION IN RELIGION.
teach.b: The Qur'an says plainly: "There is no compulsion in religion." In America that line can be heard twice: as a teaching of the faith, and as something close to the country's own promise that belief is free.
A convert chooses. An immigrant family chooses to stay. A grandchild of the old streams chooses to keep praying.

how: American Muslims gather in mosques and Islamic centers founded by immigrant, African American and convert communities, and many mosques hold open houses where neighbors can visit and ask questions.

games.q: a coworker tells you she's Muslim. what's the most useful next question?
o: so where are you really from?
how did your family come to the faith, or you?
games.why: she might be an immigrant's daughter, the grandchild of African American Muslims, or a convert. the story is the interesting part.

practice: Think of an American Muslim you know of: a neighbor, a coworker, a doctor, an athlete, a poet, someone from the news.

What do you actually know about their life beyond the label, where their family came from, or how they came to the faith? If you pray, ask God's blessing on them; if not, just let their story be bigger than the label.
